card.hook: Picture a sea of green treetops rolling away to a working canal, with a cargo ship sliding past like it's the most normal thing in the world. That's the Soberanía view, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Head up to the top observation deck of the Canopy Tower, about 50 ft above the trees. The tower is about 1.2 km east of Soberanía National Park, so the park lies to the west of you. Face out over the treetops towards the canal.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of treetops, sky and canal, then go to 1x for a calmer view. Try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the ships and the Centennial Bridge in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, and keep some treetops in the foreground to show off the height.
card.best_time: Early morning is a good bet, with softer light and more bird and animal activity. Check the official site for visiting times before you plan around it.
card.selfie_here: Try the observation tower at the Rainforest Discovery Center, a short walk in from the Pipeline Road entrance. Guides say it looks over the treetops, sometimes with a ship passing on the canal. Use the front camera, hold it a bit above eye level, and let the forest fill the background behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Canopy Tower deck is on a private lodge, so getting in may depend on being a guest or joining a tour. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Spot a ship and the Centennial Bridge in the same shot, then zoom in until they're both tiny but still easy to find.
card.good_to_know: Soberanía became a national park in 1980 and covers about 220 square kilometres. Around 525 bird species have been recorded here, and Pipeline Road, about 17.5 km long, is one of the best-known places to see them. History fans can walk parts of the Camino de Cruces, a 16th-century trail the Spanish used to move gold.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to the top observation deck of the Canopy Tower, about 50 ft above the trees. The tower is about 1.2 km east of Soberanía National Park, so the park lies to the west of you. Face out over the treetops towards the canal.

card.hook: Low buildings, moored boats and a wall of thick green jungle: this is a working science harbour, not a big-sights stop. It's quiet and moody, and it makes a lovely calm photo.
card.stand_here: Start at the Puerto de Gamboa waterfront in the Gamboa area of the map. The institute's waterfront is about 467 m to the south-west, so face south-west and stick to public paths.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole calm scene. Then try zoom 2x to pick out the buildings and moored boats without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the brightest part of the sky or water and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the greenery doesn't go gloomy.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is best, with softer light and fewer harsh glints on the water. You'll also dodge the worst of the tropical midday heat.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and turn your back to the water, so the harbour and the green hills sit over your shoulder. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the scene in, and keep the horizon level behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a research site and a working harbour, so stay on public paths and respect any signs. Access may be limited, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a boat or a bird to drift through your frame, then snap it with its reflection on still water.
card.good_to_know: The Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute is a working scientific organisation. This spot is its waterside base at Puerto de Gamboa, beside the Panama Canal. It's more about atmosphere than famous sights, so go slow and enjoy the harbour edge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the Puerto de Gamboa waterfront in the Gamboa area of the map. The institute's waterfront is about 467 m to the south-west, so face south-west and stick to public paths.

selfie_spots.detail: small concrete overlook with a railing, about halfway along the Naos Island section of the causeway
selfie_spots.why: A guide calls it the best photo spot on the causeway, and it looks out over ships queuing in the anchorage.

card.hook: Picture a straight band of water running between steep, cut-away hillsides, right through the Continental Divide. Someone dug that mountain out of the way, and you get to stand and admire it.
card.stand_here: Go to the phone icon on the map, about 85 m north of the subject (the Culebra Cut), and face south. The Navigate buttons will take you straight there.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to take in the whole width of the valley, then switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the channel. If a ship shows up, try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick it out or to get closer to the far slopes.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on the far bank, then drag the slider to make it a bit darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the slopes than midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the valley over your shoulder. Leave a bit of sky and hillside in the frame so people can see how big the cut is.
card.rules_and_safety: Access and viewing rules for the canal area may change, so check the official site before you go. Visitors report you can't stop on the Centennial Bridge, so don't count on it for your photo.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the channel on a lower third line, and try to catch a ship in the middle distance without tilting the water.
card.good_to_know: The Culebra Cut runs for 12.6 kilometres between the Pedro Miguel lock and the Chagres River arm of Gatun Lake. Digging began under the French in 1881, and steam shovels broke through on 20 May 1913. It was called Gaillard Cut from 1915 to 2000, and it's also known as the Snake Cut.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the phone icon on the map, about 85 m north of the subject (the Culebra Cut), and face south. The Navigate buttons will take you straight there.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie or photo spot with the Culebra Cut behind the visitor, so I have returned no selfie spots. The only public viewpoint named is the Centennial Bridge (Puente Centenario), which crosses the cut near Pedro Miguel. Two sources say you cannot stop on it: a Tripadvisor forum thread (https://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowTopic-g294480-i1194-k15449643-Panama_Canal_visit-Panama_City_Panama_Province.html) says the bridge is the only public viewpoint but you can't stop there, and a Tripadvisor review (https://www.tripadvisor.com/ShowUserReviews-g294480-d6354448-r357661743-Centennial_Bridge-Panama_City_Panama_Province.html) says the fencing makes photography impossible. The same forum thread says there is no public access along the Culebra Cut itself. Gold Hill and Contractor's Hill are named vantage points in historical photo collections (for example https://www.slpl.org/panama-canal-photograph-collection/ and https://exhibits.tulane.edu/exhibit/bridging-two-oceans-the-complex-legacy-of-the-panama-canal/the-culebra-cut/), but I found no current page confirming public access to either, so I did not list them. Ship-transit pages (for example https://madaboutpanama.com/panama-canal-cruise/what-you-will-see/through-the-canal/) describe the cut from the water, not a land spot. No page gave rules on selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gave a safety point for this site. The given coordinates match the Wikipedia entry for the Culebra Cut (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culebra_Cut). Visitors should check current access before going, because the sources I found are dated.

card.hook: Picture a big ship easing into the lock right in front of you, and way off behind it, two pale towers with a fan of cables. That's the Centennial Bridge, and it only looks this good when you shoot it from the right spot.
card.stand_here: Go to the Pedro Miguel locks viewing area (Esclusas de Pedro Miguel) and face the bridge, which sits about 2.5 km to the north-east of the locks. Follow the direction shown on the map and you'll be looking right at it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to bring the bridge closer. Use zoom 1x for a wider shot with the lock and a ship in it. Save zoom 0.5x for close-up details at the locks, because the bridge turns tiny there.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the picture a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out those cables.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a calmer feel. Honestly, a ship passing matters more than the hour, so wait for one if you can.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, stand with your back to the bridge and let it peek over your shoulder. It's far away, so it will look small. Let a ship or the lock fill the space beside you, and don't stop on the bridge itself for this.
card.rules_and_safety: The lock area is a working part of the canal, so access may be controlled. Check the official site before you go, and don't stop on the bridge itself.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one wide with the bridge tiny and a ship in front, and one zoomed in on just the towers. Which one tells the canal story better?
card.good_to_know: Each tower is 184 m high, and the main span is 420 m long. It clears the water by 80 m, so large ships pass easily underneath. The bridge was named for Panama's centennial in November 2003 and inaugurated on 15 August 2004, the 90th anniversary of the first ship through the canal. It opened to traffic in September 2005.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the Pedro Miguel locks viewing area (Esclusas de Pedro Miguel) and face the bridge, which sits about 2.5 km to the north-east of the locks. Follow the direction shown on the map and you'll be looking right at it.

selfie_spots.detail: Just past the bridge exit when heading out of the city; the page gives no exact name for the lookout
selfie_spots.why: A reviewer describes a pull-off there that lets visitors photograph the bridge itself, though it is not named.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported, and it is weakly located. No page names the lookout, so it is hard to find on a map. The 'lookout' comes from a single reviewer, and the same page says the bridge's views are better from the canal. Other pages say there is little or no stopping room on the bridge, so I did not add a spot there. The Tripadvisor line about a stop 'near the Chinese Monument' belongs to the Bridge of the Americas: the monument (Mirador Chino) stood there and was demolished in December 2025, so I excluded it. A travel guide lists Miraflores/Corozal as the better Centennial photo areas, but it names no specific standing point, so I did not use it as a passer-by spot. No page states any selfie-stick or tripod rule; the tripod line is only a photography tip, so I left rules empty. The given coordinates (9.03096, -79.63521) were not checked against a map.

card.hook: Picture a huge ship parked in a concrete box while the water around it slowly drops, and you're close enough to watch it happen. Fair warning: the ships take their time, so bring some patience.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits right at the subject, so you're already in the right place at the Miraflores Locks visitors centre. Stay on the viewing area or observation terrace with a clear view over the chamber, and face the lock chamber.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the chamber and ship together, then try 0.5x to catch the whole lock and the sky. Go to 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the gates and ship details, and push in further to spot the Pedro Miguel Locks way off in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the lock wall up along one of the lines so the chamber looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go when a ship is due, because that's when the locks are actually working. Ships move in set directions at set times, so ask on the day or check the official site, and be ready to wait 30 minutes or more. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
card.selfie_here: Try the ground-level terrace (Level 1) at the Miraflores Visitor Center, right at the edge overlooking the lock chambers. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it slightly up so the chamber walls and the ship's hull fit in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a kind stranger to shoot you at the front rail of the upper deck while a ship enters the lower chamber, so the locks and bridge are framed behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Bring sunscreen and water, since the upper terraces are open-air. Check current status before you visit, as the upper deck may not be open and the visitors centre is ticketed.
card.challenge: Catch the same ship twice, once as it glides in and once as the water level has changed, and see if your friends can spot the difference.
card.good_to_know: Miraflores is the set of locks closest to the Pacific end of the Panama Canal. Ships are lifted or lowered by 54 feet (16.5 m) in two stages here. That lets them pass between the Pacific port of Balboa and the little lake that leads to the Pedro Miguel Locks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits right at the subject, so you're already in the right place at the Miraflores Locks visitors centre. Stay on the viewing area or observation terrace with a clear view over the chamber, and face the lock chamber.

selfie_spots.why: You are essentially at the same elevation as the lock chamber floor, looking across at the chamber walls and the ship's hull.

card.hook: Picture a single-lane iron and wood bridge, rusty and a bit wobbly-looking, curving over a river bend. For most of Gamboa's history, this was the only way into town.
card.stand_here: Stand on the bank near the town end of Puente Viejo de Gamboa, the old single-lane bridge, and face the bridge so the river and any ships sit behind it. The marked centre of the town is about 7 minutes on foot to the north-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the bridge, river and canal waters in one shot, and let the bridge lead the eye across. Then try zoom 0.5x up close on the worn ironwork, and zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a ship or boat on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the bridge along the lower third line, and keep a bit of bank in front for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh reflections on the water. Check the sky when you arrive, because it changes with the weather and season.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the town behind you, try the top of the hilltop observation tower at Gamboa Rainforest Resort, where the view takes in the town, river and canal. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it out so the view sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the bank rather than standing on the bridge, because it's a single-lane crossing. Check whether it's still open to traffic before you stop near it.
card.challenge: Get one frame where the bridge leads across the picture and a ship or little boat is tucked into the distance.
card.good_to_know: Gamboa was built in 1911 while the canal was being dug. Its first residents were workers moved out of villages that Lake Gatun later covered. A newer two-lane bridge opened beside the old one in October 2018, but the old one is still standing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the bank near the town end of Puente Viejo de Gamboa, the old single-lane bridge, and face the bridge so the river and any ships sit behind it. The marked centre of the town is about 7 minutes on foot to the north-west.

The bridge is also a working railway and road crossing; one page describes an older single-lane bridge that was a rough crossing, and a newer bridge was completed in 2018, so check which one you mean.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: the best view of a giant ship at Pedro Miguel is through a chain-link fence. No visitor centre, no platform, just a roadside strip and a working canal right in front of you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the roadside parking strip on the main road beside Pedro Miguel Locks, right where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the lock chamber and look for a gap in the fence, with the Centenary Bridge and the Gaillard Cut entrance off to your right.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x with your phone held close to a gap in the fence. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a ship or the lock gates. Skip zoom 0.5x here, because it mostly shows fence.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the ship (not the fence), then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and water keep their colour.
card.best_time: One guide says ships are typically processed from east to west in the afternoon, so aim for later in the day. Ship movements vary, so give yourself time to wait for one to slide into your gap.
card.selfie_here: Try the large parking area in front of the locks, where the lock chamber is the backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the lock over your shoulder. We haven't confirmed this one on the ground, so have a quick look around first.
card.ask_someone: Onlookers watch ships from the parking strip about 100 m past the locks on the highway toward Gamboa, so it's a good place to ask a fellow ship-watcher to snap you.
card.rules_and_safety: The fence is too high to shoot over, so photograph through the gaps and keep your camera just clear of the wire. Take care with traffic when you get out. Whether the fence and parking stay open isn't certain, so check local conditions first. If you fancy the Luisa Hill lookout for a wider view, check it's open before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a ship's bow perfectly framed in one fence gap, with the bridge peeking in on the right. Bonus points if the wire disappears completely.
card.good_to_know: Pedro Miguel is the single-step lock site on the Panama Canal. Its 31-foot (9.4-metre) lift is the smallest on the route, and the locks opened in 1914. Each chamber is 1,050 feet (320 metres) long and 110 feet (33.5 metres) wide, and little electric locomotives called mules run along the walls to steady the ships.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the roadside parking strip on the main road beside Pedro Miguel Locks, right where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the lock chamber and look for a gap in the fence, with the Centenary Bridge and the Gaillard Cut entrance off to your right.

selfie_spots.why: This is the one open spot that pages describe as giving a close view of the chamber, so a selfie taken here can keep the lock in frame behind the visitor (my inference, not a page's claim).

card.hook: Picture a big, serious harpy eagle looking straight at you while you hold a phone about the size of its snack. That's the main event at Parque Municipal Summit, tucked into the tropical forest beside Soberania National Park.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map marks the centre of the park, so start there. Then walk to the harpy eagle compound inside the grounds and face the eagle's enclosure.
card.zoom: Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the eagle, so you can stay back from the wire. Switch to 1x for the bamboo tunnel and 0.5x if you want the whole pond and its green frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the eagle's eye, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the feathers keep their detail.
card.best_time: Check the official site for visiting times before you go, because pages disagree on them. As general advice, morning light is softer and the air is cooler for walking. The bamboo tunnel is shaded, so it's a good fallback when the sun is strong.
card.selfie_here: We don't have a named selfie spot here, so keep it simple. Use the front camera, hold it a little higher than your face, and let the leafy green of the garden fill in behind your shoulder. The bamboo tunnel makes a nice backdrop if you stand at one end.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed, but follow posted signs and staff instructions, especially near sensitive exhibits. Keep a respectful distance from wildlife and stay on marked paths. Entry rules, fees and opening times may apply, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Wire fighting you? Take the eagle at three different distances and see which frame makes the mesh disappear. Winner gets bragging rights.
card.good_to_know: The park began in 1923 as an experimental farm run by the Panama Canal company, testing how plants from around the world coped with Panama's climate. Teak reached the Americas through that farm. The zoo started in the 1960s and now has about 300 animals. The harpy eagle is Panama's national bird.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map marks the centre of the park, so start there. Then walk to the harpy eagle compound inside the grounds and face the eagle's enclosure.

rules.rule: Photography is generally allowed at the park, but visitors should follow posted signs and staff instructions, especially near sensitive exhibits.

selfie_research.safety: Keep a respectful distance from wildlife and stay on marked paths to protect the habitat.
selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot or photo spot could be found that a page names by a mappable name. Pages mention 'monkey enclosures' as popular for photos and 'the lush botanical gardens' as backdrops, but none say where to stand with the landmark behind you, and no page describes a spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole park in frame, so both fields are empty. The city field reads 'Panama Canal', which is not a city; the park is in the Summit/Ancón area of Panama City, Panamá Province, and the given coordinates match the park's listed position. Opening hours differ between pages (9 AM to 3 PM, 9 AM to 4 PM, 9 AM to 5 PM), so check before going. No page states any rule about selfie sticks or tripods, so none is reported. Only one search was run for photo spots, so a local photo guide or the park's own site (mupa.gob.pa/summit) may name spots not covered here.
